messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Environmental Scientist
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Breathing): Heavy breathing sounds, Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed, Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Farid Hassan is a 78-year-old married environmental scientist who came to treatment after months of feeling as though one part of his life had become impossible to put into words. He is a Lebanese American man who has spent decades in field-based environmental work, and even in retirement he still consults part time, reviewing site reports and occasionally visiting restoration projects with younger staff. He described the event that troubles him as an accident in which another person was seriously injured and in which, as he says with visible strain, “I was the one who did it.” Yet whenever he tries to tell the story from beginning to end, he stalls. He knows what happened, can circle around parts of it, but then the language seems to drop away. He becomes quiet, shakes his head, and says that the facts are in his mind but will not come out in order.

From the fragments he has been able to give, the accident occurred during work-related activity when another person was badly hurt as a result of something Farid did. What stands out most in his recollection is not a neat sequence but a series of sensory moments that return with force. He remembers the other man’s breathing after the injury: loud, labored, uneven breathing that cut through everything else around them. In session, when he came near that part of the memory, Farid’s posture changed abruptly, as if he were no longer in the office. He stared ahead and spoke in the present tense, saying it is like “I am there again,” hearing that breathing and waiting for what comes next. At those moments the memory does not feel like a past event he is recalling; it feels immediate and current, as though the accident is happening again in front of him. At other times, he speaks about it with a kind of disbelief, saying the whole thing is so extreme that it is hard to accept that it actually happened to him, that this could really be part of his own life.

In the weeks after the accident, Farid found that ordinary moments could shift suddenly into something terrifying. Heavy breathing was the clearest example. If he heard someone out of breath climbing stairs, if a person at a medical clinic exhaled loudly nearby, or if a recording in a documentary picked up strained respiration, his body reacted before he could steady himself. He would feel himself pulled back into the scene of the injury. Because he still spent time with environmental colleagues on site visits, he began dreading moments that once would have gone unnoticed, such as walking behind a coworker on a steep path and hearing exertion in the other person’s breathing. He tried to stand farther away, let others walk ahead, or stay back at the vehicle longer than necessary. These changes were noticeable enough that a younger colleague asked whether he was feeling physically well.

What unsettled Farid almost as much was that the reaction was not limited to obviously dangerous situations. He discovered that feeling relaxed or happy could also bring the accident sharply to mind. Sitting on his back patio after dinner with his wife, during the brief ease of an ordinary evening, he would suddenly feel exposed, as though he had let his guard down and been caught by the memory. The shift was jarring: one second he was content, the next he was back at the scene. Over time he became wary of those lighter moments, never saying so directly to his family but pulling back from them in small ways. He would cut short pleasant outings, keep conversations practical, and remain watchful when things felt too calm.

Physical affection also became difficult. When his wife embraced him, especially if she held him closely against her chest, Farid sometimes froze. He described the closeness, warmth, and bodily awareness of another person’s breathing as enough to set off the same sense of immediacy. He began to turn hugs into quick pats on the shoulder or found reasons to keep moving when she approached him affectionately. This change hurt her, and he could see that it did, but he could not explain it clearly because the account kept collapsing at the point where he most wanted to explain himself.

By the time he sought help, Farid was living with the sense that he could be taken over by the memory in moments that should have been safe: at home with his wife, in the ordinary satisfactions of a good day, or while accompanying colleagues in the field that had defined his career. What finally brought him in was a recent family gathering when, in the middle of laughter and a hug from one of his adult children, he was abruptly overwhelmed by the feeling that the accident was happening again. He pulled away so suddenly that everyone noticed. Now he says he wants, more than anything, to be able to be with his family without bracing himself and to tell the story of what happened without losing the words, though he is frightened that if he gets too close to it, he will be right back there hearing that breathing again.
